title: Structural-Entropy-Based Sample Selection for Efficient and Effective Learning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to incorporate global graph structure into sample selection, addressing the limitation of existing methods that rely solely on local information. Paper [2] explicitly mentions designing a structure entropy-based node importance ranking method that incorporates global structure information, which aligns with the same objective of leveraging global graph structure. Paper [19] discusses subset selection on graphs but focuses on computational efficiency rather than incorporating global graph structure, so it does not match the purpose. No other paper explicitly addresses the same problem-class level objective.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces a node-level structural entropy metric derived from graph-level structural entropy using the Shapley value, reformulated for linear-time computation. Paper [10] discusses efficient computation of the Shapley value for game-theoretic network centrality, which overlaps with the use of Shapley values for graph-related tasks. However, it does not reformulate the Shapley value for structural entropy or address linear-time computation. Paper [17] uses structural entropy optimization for graph structure learning but does not decompose graph-level structural entropy to individual nodes or reformulate the Shapley value. Paper [2] uses structural entropy but does not employ Shapley values or linear-time computation. No prior paper matches the mechanism at the primitive level.

### Evaluation
The contribution validates its method theoretically and empirically, showing that maximizing node-level structural entropy improves sample coverage. Paper [19] uses subset selection on graphs and validates computational efficiency, but it does not use the same evaluation design (theoretical bound ratio or synthetic data matching CIFAR10 stats). Paper [17] validates structural entropy optimization but does not use the same evaluation design. No prior paper employs the same theoretical bound ratio or synthetic data setup, making the evaluation design novel.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of sample selection/data-efficient learning. Paper [19] explicitly addresses subset selection on graphs, which falls within the same general application area. Paper [21] discusses coreset selection, which is also a form of sample selection for data-efficient learning. Both papers cover the domain facet.

Paper [3] ("Structural Entropy Based Graph Node Classification") introduces structural entropy as a measure of uncertainty in graph structures, which is equivalent to the global scoring primitive. Paper [5] ("Density Aware Blue-Noise Sampling on Graphs") extends blue-noise sampling to irregular graphs, which matches the importance-biased blue noise sampling primitive. Together, these papers cover the mechanism's core primitives.

The evaluation design includes ablation experiments showing the complementary benefits of structural entropy and blue noise sampling, as well as comparisons to D2Pruning. Paper [23] ("DeepCore: A Comprehensive Library for Coreset Selection in Deep Learning") uses ablation studies to validate coreset selection methods, which matches the evaluation design of isolating component contributions. Paper [25] ("Data pruning and neural scaling laws") also uses ablation and score-based comparisons to validate pruning methods, aligning with the evaluation design. These prior works cover the evaluation design.

The domain is sample selection in supervised, active, or continual learning. Paper [23] ("DeepCore") explicitly addresses coreset selection for deep learning, which is a subset of sample selection. Papers [23] and [24] directly address coreset/subset selection for deep learning — [23] states "coreset selection, which aims to select a subset of the most informative training samples" and [24] "strives to identify a small subset from large-scale data." Paper [11] also addresses "selecting a small set of the most informative examples from a large unlabeled pool." The combination of "global and local signals" is a refinement of the same objective (select informative+representative samples under budget), not a new problem class. Paper [22] addresses "sample selection for maximal diversity." These papers cover the same objective at the problem-class level.

## Mechanism: kNN graph → structural entropy (global) × training difficulty (local) → importance-biased blue noise sampling for iterative diverse selection.

Breaking this down:
- **kNN graph + structural entropy scoring**: Papers [3], [4], [6], [14] all use structural entropy on graphs, but none apply it to score training sample importance for dataset pruning. Paper [3] uses SE for node classification; [4] for graph structure learning.
- **Training difficulty as local signal**: Papers [23], [24] use training difficulty metrics (e.g., forgetting scores, EL2N) for coreset selection.
- **Blue noise sampling on graphs**: Papers [5] and [15] introduce blue noise sampling on graphs. Paper [5] explicitly presents "density aware blue-noise sampling on graphs." Paper [15] discusses "blue noise sampling... on graphs."
- **Importance-biased blue noise**: Paper [10] does multi-class blue noise; papers [17], [18] do blue noise variants. None combine structural entropy × training difficulty as the importance score fed into graph blue noise sampling.

The specific combination — (1) building a kNN sample graph, (2) scoring via structural entropy (global) × training difficulty (local), and (3) using importance-biased blue noise sampling on that graph — is not found as a unified primitive in any prior paper. Individual components appear (SE in [3]/[4]/[6], blue noise on graphs in [5]/[15], training difficulty in [23]/[24]), but the composite mechanism is absent.

## Evaluation: Ablation showing SE and BNS are complementary components, BNS matches D2Pruning without grid search.

Papers [23] and [24] both perform ablation studies on coreset selection methods, comparing components and baselines. The evaluation design — ablation table comparing individual components (SE, BNS) against a baseline and against each other — is a standard ablation design used in [23] and [24] for the same claim type (which components contribute to coreset selection performance). The comparison against D2Pruning is a substitution/swap experiment within the same benchmark family used in [23]/[24]. This is a covered evaluation design.

## Domain: Sample selection (supervised/active/continual learning)

Papers [23], [24], [11], [16], [9], [7] all operate in sample selection / active learning / coreset selection for deep learning. This domain is clearly covered.
